items.title: Hermes Agent Plugins Marketplace: One-Click Plugins for Hermes Desktop
items.content:
The Hermes Agent plugins marketplace lets you install community plugins into Hermes Desktop in one click — voice like Jarvis, a live news feed, job search, multi-device control and hundreds more, all free. In the video below I install a few live. Here’s how the marketplace works and the one check you must do before installing anything.

Key takeaways

- The official plugin catalogue lives on the Hermes Agent docs site and inside Hermes Desktop’s capabilities section.

- It has official and community plugins — around 500 when I recorded.

- Click Open in Hermes Desktop, choose a profile, and install.

- Always check the GitHub repo before installing a community plugin.

## What the Hermes Agent plugins marketplace is

Nous Research launched an official plugin catalogue for Hermes Agent, which you can reach on the Hermes Agent docs site or in the capabilities section of Hermes Desktop. It started with a handful of official plugins and around a hundred community ones, and it has grown fast — I counted about 500 when I recorded.

Each listing shows its star rating, when it was last updated and its version, and you can filter by category — memory, voice, messaging, browsing, desktop panes and more. Nous says it reviews community plugins, and anyone can submit their own.

## How to install from the Hermes Agent plugins marketplace

- Browse the catalogue and open a plugin.

- Click Open in Hermes Desktop, then Open Hermes.

- Choose where it appears (for example, in the desktop UI) and which profile gets it.

- Click Install — done.

I installed Hermes Newswire this way. In its settings I added a topic — “Hermes Agent” — searched for release notes, and within seconds there was a scrolling news feed along the bottom of my chats. You can add sources, change the speed, pause it or switch it off.

## Best plugins I found in the Hermes Agent plugins marketplace

Plugin
What it does

Hermes Newswire
A live news ticker in Hermes Desktop — add topics like “Hermes Agent release notes” and sources, set speed, pause it

Hermes Tailscale
Connect and control Hermes across several devices over Tailscale

Voice plugins (speech, talk, live voice)
Talk to Hermes like Jarvis — install one, not all of them

Job search
Hyper-personalised job search that filters postings by what matters to you

Hermes Office 2
A visual office where you can watch your agents work

Platform gateways
WhatsApp, and even a Minecraft gateway

Search tools
Brave Search, Ollama Cloud web search and browser automations

You don’t need all of them. Pick the ones that fit how you work — and for categories with lots of options, like voice, I’d choose the one with the most stars.

## Why plugins beat the old terminal setup

Before this, adding a capability to Hermes meant the terminal, config files and sometimes three hours on a GitHub skill that didn’t even work. Now it’s one click, and the ratings help you skip the dead ones. If you still want the manual route, each plugin page has its installation instructions and README.

For connecting apps like Gmail or Notion, see my Hermes Agent connectors guide — and for a solid base setup, my best Hermes setup walkthrough.

## Check every plugin before you install it

Community plugins are open-source projects written by anyone. Check them before you install — a plugin runs with your agent’s access.

- Open the GitHub repository before you install and read the README — what it does, what it needs access to.

- Check the stars and last-updated date in the catalogue; abandoned plugins break.

- Install into a test profile first — Hermes lets you choose which profile a plugin goes into.

- Pick one plugin per job — one voice plugin, not five.

- Never paste keys into a plugin you haven’t vetted.

## Plugins vs skills vs connectors in Hermes

Type
What it is
Example

Plugin
Code that adds features to Hermes or Hermes Desktop
Newswire, Tailscale, voice

Skill
A set of instructions and scripts the agent follows for a task
An SEO audit procedure

Connector
A link to an outside app or account
Gmail, Notion, GitHub

Plugins change what Hermes itself can do; skills teach it how to do a job; connectors give it access to your apps. You’ll often use all three together. For memory specifically, see my Hermes memory plugins guide.

## My starter set of Hermes plugins

- One voice plugin — the most-starred one, so you can talk to Hermes hands-free.

- Hermes Newswire — set to your niche, so news comes to you.

- Hermes Tailscale — if you use Hermes on more than one device.

- A search plugin — Brave Search is a good free option.

- Hermes Office 2 — if you like seeing your agents work visually.

Five plugins, each solving one problem. Add more only when you have a specific need. Fewer plugins means fewer things to update and fewer things that can break.

## How to remove or update a Hermes plugin

Plugins aren’t permanent. Each one has its own settings page in Hermes Desktop where you can switch it on or off without uninstalling it — handy for testing whether a plugin is causing a problem. If you don’t use a plugin any more, uninstall it rather than leaving it switched off.

Check the catalogue now and then for updates: the last-updated date tells you whether a plugin is still maintained. If Hermes starts behaving oddly after an update, switch off the plugins you added most recently one at a time until you find the culprit. Keeping a spare test profile makes all of this painless.

## The bottom line on the Hermes Agent plugins marketplace

The Hermes Agent plugins marketplace makes Hermes Desktop feel like a brand-new app built exactly for you — free, one-click, and growing every week. Check the repo, test in a spare profile, and install only what you’ll actually use.

Yes — the catalogue has a submission link for developers.

items.content:
Solar Mini 4 Hermes setup takes a few clicks, and right now Upstage’s new model is free inside Hermes Agent for a limited window. In the video below I set it up in Hermes Cloud, Hermes Desktop and Agent OS — and show the one setting you must get right, or you’ll end up on the paid version by accident.

Key takeaways

- Solar Mini 4 is free in Hermes Agent for a limited time, from 5 October 2026.

- It’s listed under the Free models in Nous Portal.

- I give each model its own Hermes profile so I can switch fast.

- Select the free version — the plain Solar Mini 4 entry is the paid one.

## Why use Solar Mini 4 with Hermes

Solar Mini 4 is Upstage’s fast agent model — 3B active parameters out of 35B, 512K context — and Nous Research is offering it free in Hermes Agent for a limited time. My Solar Mini 4 overview covers the specs and benchmarks; this page is purely about getting it running in Hermes.

It’s not a frontier model, but for research, summaries and everyday agent tasks it’s fast and costs nothing.

## Solar Mini 4 Hermes setup in Hermes Cloud

- Go to Nous Portal’s cloud page and create an agent.

- Scroll to the model section and click Free.

- Choose Upstage Solar Mini 4.

- Deploy — your Hermes instance now runs in the cloud on a free model.

You’ll see other free models in the same list, so you have backups ready.

Want this working in your business, not just bookmarked? Setting up Hermes Agent with free models is exactly what we build together inside the AI Profit Boardroom — 3,400+ members, four live calls a week, and a full one-hour DeepSeek Harness course in the classroom.

Prefer it mapped 1-on-1 first? Book a free strategy session and we’ll plan it for your exact situation.

## Solar Mini 4 Hermes setup in Hermes Desktop

- Open Hermes Desktop and create a new profile — I name it after the model, “solar mini 4”.

- Open the model settings and refresh the model list.

- Edit the models and select Solar Mini 4 from the free models.

- Send a test message — mine replied instantly.

Why a new profile? I keep one profile per model so I can switch and compare in seconds without breaking my main setup. You can use an existing profile if you prefer.

## Using Solar Mini 4 in the Hermes dashboard or Agent OS

If you run the dashboard, type `hermes dashboard` in your terminal, open Models, choose Set main model, search “solar”, go to the Nous Portal section and pick the free Solar Mini 4. Inside Agent OS, add the Solar Mini 4 profile under Hermes and chat with it directly.

The setting that matters: in the model list there’s a free Solar Mini 4 and a paid one. Pick the version marked free. If you choose the other entry, you’re on the paid model.

## Other free models and rate limits

Free models can get rate limited. If that happens, refresh the model list and switch to another free model. The free list in Nous Portal when I recorded included:

- Upstage Solar Mini 4

- Poolside Laguna XS 2.1

- inclusionAI Ling 3.1 Flash and Ling 3.0 Flash

- StepFun Step 3.7 Flash

- Meituan LongCat 2.0

That’s why the one-profile-per-model setup is so useful — switching takes seconds.

## Solar Mini 4 Hermes troubleshooting

- Solar Mini 4 isn’t in the list — refresh the model list; new free models don’t always show until you do.

- Unexpected charges — you’ve picked the paid entry. Switch to the free one under Nous Portal.

- Rate limit errors — wait a few minutes or switch profile to another free model.

- Memory is off — a new profile starts with memory switched off; turn it on in the profile settings if you want it.

- Slow replies in Agent OS — check you’ve selected the Solar Mini 4 profile, not your default one.

## What to use Solar Mini 4 for in Hermes

It handles basic agentic tasks well. The jobs I’d give it:

- Daily AI news research and summaries

- Researching competitors or topics before a piece of content

- Turning notes and transcripts into structured outlines

- Simple scheduled tasks that run every day

For hard coding or complex reasoning, switch profile to a frontier model like Claude Opus 5.5. That’s the whole point of one profile per model: the right brain for each job, one click apart. If you want more free options, my Ling 3.0 Flash guide covers another free model in the same list.

## Why I keep one Hermes profile per model

It sounds like extra admin, but it saves me time every day. Each profile remembers its own model, settings and history, so switching from Solar Mini 4 to Claude Opus 5.5 or another free model is a single click — no digging through settings, no breaking the setup I rely on.

It also makes testing honest. When a new model drops, I create a profile, run the same task I ran on the others — my standard is “research the last seven days of AI automation news” — and compare the answers side by side. That’s how I decided Solar Mini 4 is good enough for everyday research but not for hard reasoning. When the free window closes, I simply switch that profile to the next free model.

## Is Solar Mini 4 Hermes worth setting up?

Yes — it takes a couple of minutes, it’s fast, and it’s free while the window lasts. My research test came back quickly with a clear, well-sourced breakdown. Set up a Solar Mini 4 Hermes profile today and make sure you select the free version.

One more tip: note the date you set it up. Free windows end, and when this one does your Solar Mini 4 profile will stop answering or start charging. When that happens, open the profile and switch it to whichever free model is current.

Create a new Hermes profile, refresh the model list and select the free Solar Mini 4 from Nous Portal’s free models.

Yes, for a limited time from 5 October 2026 — as long as you select the free version.

You probably selected the paid entry. Switch to the version marked free in the model list.

### What if Solar Mini 4 is rate limited?

Refresh the model list and switch to another free model like Ling 3.1 Flash or Step 3.7 Flash.

Yes — add your Solar Mini 4 Hermes profile in Agent OS, or set it as the main model in the Hermes dashboard.

Solar Mini 4 Hermes setup in Hermes Desktop

Using Solar Mini 4 in the Hermes dashboard or Agent OS

If you run the dashboard, type hermes dashboard in your terminal, open Models, choose Set main model, search “solar”, go to the Nous Portal section and pick the free Solar Mini 4. Inside Agent OS, add the Solar Mini 4 profile under Hermes and chat with it directly.

items.content:
Solar Mini 4 is Upstage’s new agent model — 35 billion parameters, only 3 billion active, a 512K-token context window, and right now you can use it free inside Hermes Agent. I tested it in the video below on a real research task. Here are the specs, the benchmarks, the price and my honest take.

Key takeaways

- Solar Mini 4 is a 35B mixture-of-experts model with 3B active parameters, from South Korea’s Upstage.

- It has a 512K context window and up to 128K output tokens.

- It scored 24.1 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index.

- Standard API pricing is $0.10/$0.40 per million tokens — and it’s free in Hermes Agent for a limited time.

## What Solar Mini 4 is

Upstage is a South Korean AI company, and Solar Mini 4 is a model it pretrained from scratch specifically for agents — high-volume, repetitive work like retrieving information, producing structured output and calling tools, at low cost. Because it’s a mixture-of-experts model, only 3 billion of its 35 billion parameters are used for each token, which is why it’s so fast.

In my test I asked it to research the last seven days of AI automation news. It came back quickly with a tidy breakdown — sources, what stands out, the key stories. It even surfaced a launch I hadn’t seen. Upstage quotes 70+ tokens per second on two H100 GPUs.

Let me be 100% honest: this is not a frontier model. You won’t use it the way you use Claude Opus 5.5 for hard reasoning. But for basic agentic tasks — research, summaries, structured output — it’s more than good enough, and it’s fast.

## Solar Mini 4 pricing and where to use it

Standard pricing is $0.10 per million input tokens, $0.01 per million cached input tokens and $0.40 per million output tokens, and Upstage ran a 70% launch discount until 10 October 2026. You can use it through the Upstage Console API, Solar Chat, OpenRouter, on-premises, and inside Hermes Agent.

The best deal right now: Hermes Agent users get it free for a limited window, which opened on 5 October. My step-by-step Solar Mini 4 Hermes guide shows exactly how to set it up — and the one setting that stops you landing on the paid version by accident.

## Who should use Solar Mini 4

- Hermes Agent users who want a fast free model for everyday tasks

- Builders running lots of agent calls who care about cost per task

- Long-document work — the 512K context fits huge inputs

- Korean-language work — Upstage builds with native Korean in mind

If you need deep reasoning or complex coding, pair it with a frontier model and use Solar Mini 4 for the high-volume grunt work.

Solar Mini 4’s edge is the combination of speed, a huge context window and a very low price, with strong tool use for its size. If you want open weights you can run yourself, look at Kolibri AI. If you want the fastest thing on a Mac, a tiny local model like LFM 2.5 is hard to beat.

## Solar Mini 4 use cases I’d try

- Daily news research — the exact test I ran in the video.

- Summarising long documents — the 512K context swallows big PDFs and transcripts.

- Structured data extraction — JSON mode and structured outputs are built in.

- First-draft content briefs — fast and cheap to iterate.

- Sub-agent work — let a frontier model plan, and Solar Mini 4 do the repetitive steps.

The pattern that works: give the cheap, fast model the high-volume tasks and save the expensive model for the decisions.

## Getting the best results from Solar Mini 4

Small, fast models reward clear instructions. A few habits that help:

- Be specific — say exactly what you want back, how long, and in what format.

- Ask for structure — tables, bullet points or JSON play to its strengths.

- Give it the source material — with 512K of context, paste the documents rather than relying on what it knows.

- Check the facts — like any model, it can be confidently wrong, so verify anything important.

- Escalate when needed — if it struggles on a hard problem, switch to a frontier model rather than re-prompting forever.

## My verdict on Solar Mini 4

Solar Mini 4 is a fast, cheap, capable agent model, and while it’s free in Hermes there’s no reason not to try it. Just remember it can get rate limited — keep another free model ready to switch to.

items.title: StarNet AI Agent: The Free Pixel-Art Agent Office, Tested
items.content:
StarNet AI agent is a free, open-source agent harness that turns your AI agents into characters living on a pixel-art space station — and it’s the smoothest “agent office” I’ve tested so far. I set it up from scratch in the video below: creating an agent, plugging in a model, adding skills and apps, and recruiting a crew. Here’s everything I learned.

Key takeaways

- StarNet is free and MIT-licensed, for Windows and macOS.

- You can use your existing subscriptions, an OpenRouter key, or local models through Ollama.

- Each agent gets its own model, personality, permissions, memory and workspace.

- Add apps, skills and a whole crew — then watch them work on the station.

## What the StarNet AI agent harness is

StarNet describes itself as a living pixel-art station where real AI agents do real work. Under the cute graphics it’s a proper local-first desktop harness: you bring your own model, and each agent is a genuinely separate run with real model calls, real tools and real cost.

The clever bit is that the station isn’t decoration. A room is a team with a specific set of capabilities, a hallway is a lane where one agent is allowed to hand work to another, and an object you place in a room is an actual permission. So what you see on screen is what your agents can actually do.

## How I set up my first StarNet AI agent

Creating an agent took me one or two clicks:

- Name it and pick an appearance.

- Choose a personality — warm, dry, composed or unhinged.

- Set the approval level — I chose “ask for approval” so it doesn’t do anything crazy in the background.

- Connect a brain — sign in with a provider, paste an API key, or point it at a local model.

- Pick the model and reasoning level — low, medium, high or max.

In the video I signed in with Grok and picked Grok 4.7 — I wasn’t impressed with 4.6. Then the agent wakes up with a nice animation and asks what direction to give the station. I told it I wanted help with SEO for the AI Profit Boardroom, and it started asking sensible follow-up questions. There’s a slight delay when you send messages, so don’t panic if it takes a second.

## StarNet features worth knowing

- Agents with personalities — name, appearance, personality (warm, dry, composed or unhinged), model and reasoning level.

- Approval levels — “ask for approval” or full power, plus per-agent access to the web and local files.

- A station that reflects real state — rooms are capability-scoped teams, hallways are handoff lanes, and placed objects are real capability grants.

- Apps and widgets — connect Gmail, Notion, GitHub and more from a catalogue, many with direct sign-in.

- Skills and a framework library — install skills from the market and switch procedures like decision frameworks or content humanising on and off.

- Crew — recruit a strategist, chief of staff, researcher or marketer and summon them into the station alongside your first agent.

- Tasks, quests and levels — agents level up the more you use them, and you can track work as tasks and quests.

You can zoom in and out of the station, open the four docks where everything you run lives, and click into any agent to see its brief, growth, history and saved memories. It’s like a Tamagotchi for AI agents — and you can change the model, personality, instructions or permissions at any time.

## Apps, skills and the framework library

The app catalogue goes deep. You can add Gmail, Notion, GitHub and loads more — most with direct sign-in, some with an API key. Some apps even reach into the physical world, like finding flights or sending real letters.

Then there’s the skill market (things like ad copy testing or calendar scheduling) and the skill library, which holds procedures your agent follows — a decision framework for hard technical problems, planning, humanising content, handling hard conversations. You switch each one on or off.

## Recruiting a crew in StarNet

Once your first agent is running you can give it friends. Under Crew → Recruit you pick a role — strategist, chief of staff, researcher or marketer — give it a name and look, then either deploy it (overwriting an existing agent’s setup) or summon it as a new agent. I summoned a marketer and it appeared on the station right next to my first agent.

It reminds me of a more fun version of Paperclip — and it gave me the same “this is different” feeling I had the first time I used Hermes Agent.

## StarNet vs other AI agent offices

Tool
What it’s like
Best for

StarNet

Fun, visual multi-agent setups with your own models

Hermes Agent Office

Hermes users who want to see their agents

Paperclip
An org-chart style tool for running agent ‘companies’
Structured multi-agent teams

Of the visual agent offices I’ve tested, StarNet is the most polished and the most fun. Paperclip feels more like a spreadsheet of agents; StarNet feels like a game you happen to get work out of. If you live inside Hermes, the Hermes Agent office plugin is the closest equivalent.

My tip: start with one agent and one clear job — SEO research, a daily brief, inbox triage — before you build a crew. Every agent makes real model calls, so a big crew on a paid model adds up fast. Set a budget, use ask-for-approval mode, and only grant the access each agent needs.

## Is the StarNet AI agent worth using?

Honestly, I think it’s mostly fun right now — I wouldn’t say there are loads of practical use cases yet. But it’s the smoothest visual agent office I’ve tried, it’s free, and it works with the models you already pay for. If you want to see the code or build it yourself, read my StarNet GitHub guide. And if you’re a Hermes user: several viewers asked about using Hermes with StarNet — it isn’t a built-in provider today, so treat them as two separate tools.

If you want a free agent office that’s genuinely enjoyable to use, the StarNet AI agent harness is worth an afternoon.

items.title: Kolibri AI: Germany’s Free 78B Open-Weight Model, Explained
items.content:

items.content:
StarNet GitHub is where the free pixel-art AI agent station lives — and with dozens of forks floating around, it’s worth knowing which repo is the real one and how to get it running. Below I walk through the official repository, the downloads, running it from source, and connecting free local models. My full walkthrough of the app is in the video.

Key takeaways

- The official repo is github.com/androoAGI/starnet (1.2K+ stars at the time of writing).

- Grab installers from the starnet-releases page, or run from source with Node.js.

- Run free local models through Ollama on 127.0.0.1:11434.

- The code is MIT; the StarNet name, logo and art are not licensed for forks.

## The official StarNet GitHub repository

Search GitHub and you’ll find lots of copies of StarNet — they’re forks. The original is androoAGI/starnet, and the official site is starnetos.com. Install from the original or its releases page, not a random fork, because a fork can contain anything.

StarNet at a glance

What it is
A local-first desktop agent harness with a pixel-art space station interface

Price
Free — MIT-licensed open source (code only)

Platforms
Windows 10/11 (64-bit) and macOS (Apple Silicon and Intel)

Models
OpenRouter key, sign-in with Anthropic, OpenAI or Google accounts, or local models through Ollama

Official site
starnetos.com

Source code
github.com/androoAGI/starnet

## How to install StarNet from GitHub

The easy way: download the installer for your platform from the `androoAGI/starnet-releases` releases page — Windows 10/11 64-bit or macOS (Apple Silicon or Intel).

From source: you need Node.js 18+ and Git. Then run:

```
git clone https://github.com/androoAGI/starnet.git
cd starnet
node sidecar/index.js
```

Then open `http://localhost:8787` in your browser.

Building the desktop app yourself also needs Rust and the Tauri prerequisites:

```
npm ci
npm run desktop:dev
npm run desktop:build
```

## Running StarNet with free local models

StarNet supports Ollama out of the box. Install Ollama, pull a model — the README uses `ollama pull qwen3:8b` — and choose the OLLAMA provider when you connect your agent’s brain. StarNet talks to Ollama on `127.0.0.1:11434`, so everything stays on your machine.

Prefer a cloud model? Paste an OpenRouter key, or sign in with Anthropic, OpenAI or Google. Keys are stored by your operating system.

## What’s in the StarNet GitHub project

- Concurrent multi-agent runs, each with its own workspace, transcript and memory

- Task Briefs, recipes, reusable skills and cron scheduling

- Telegram, Discord, Slack, Signal and Matrix integrations

- A Night Shift mode for running work while you’re away

- Real file deliverables in an OUTBOX

- MCP connector support, voice push-to-talk, and spend ledgers with budgets

Spend ledgers and budgets matter: every agent run makes real model calls, so set a budget before you summon a big crew.

## StarNet licence and safety tips

The code is MIT-licensed, so you can use and modify it freely. The StarNet branding, logo and artwork are not — forks can’t reuse them. Because agents can get access to the web and your local files, start with “ask for approval” mode and only grant the permissions each agent needs.

If you’re reporting a bug or requesting a feature, the GitHub issues tab is the place — and it’s worth reading open issues before you install, to see what’s currently broken.

## StarNet GitHub troubleshooting

- localhost:8787 won’t load — check the sidecar is still running in your terminal and that nothing else is using port 8787.

- Node errors on start — confirm `node -v` shows 18 or higher.

- Ollama models don’t appear — make sure Ollama is running and you’ve pulled a model, then pick the OLLAMA provider again.

- Desktop build fails — install Rust and the Tauri prerequisites for your platform first.

- On Linux — it isn’t a supported public release target, so expect rough edges if you build it yourself.

If you’re stuck, search the repo’s issues for your error message before opening a new one — someone has often hit it already.

## Release build or source build?

Option
Pros
Cons

Installer from starnet-releases
One click, signed builds, automatic updates path
Less control

Run from source (node sidecar)
See the code, try the latest changes, runs in the browser
Needs Node and Git; you update it yourself

Build the desktop app yourself
Full control over the build
Needs Rust and Tauri; slowest to set up

For most people the installer is the right call. Run from source only if you want to read the code or contribute. Either way, check you’re on the original androoAGI repo, not a fork.

## What to build with StarNet once it’s running

Installing it is the easy part; the value comes from giving your agents real, repeatable jobs. Three I’d start with:

- A daily brief agent — connect your email and calendar, and have it summarise your day every morning.

- A research agent — give it web access and a niche, and let it gather the week’s news into a file in the OUTBOX.

- A content crew — summon a researcher and a marketer, and hand off from one to the other along a hallway.

Use Night Shift for jobs that can run while you sleep, and cron scheduling for anything that repeats. Keep each agent’s permissions tight, and check the spend ledger after the first week so you know what your setup actually costs.

Once it’s installed, my StarNet AI agent guide walks through creating your first agent, adding apps and skills, and recruiting a crew. Start with the official StarNet GitHub repo, run a local model, and you’ve got a free agent station on your own machine.

Check the owner name, look for the “forked from” line under the repo title, and compare the latest commit date with the original. The Hark AI agent launched this week as “an operating system for your life” — and it’s the cleanest AI agent I’ve used. It reads your inbox, suggests what to do next, books restaurants, plans trips and builds little dashboards for anything you want to track. - It’s proactive — it reads your email and suggests action items you approve with yes or no.

- Panels are custom mini-apps, Projects handle long tasks, and you can schedule tasks.

- There’s a free plan; paid tiers are $20/month (2× usage) and $100/month (10×).

## What the Hark AI agent is

Hark is a new consumer AI company founded by Brett Adcock, who also founded the robotics company Figure. Its first product, Hark Pro, is an AI assistant that connects to your email, calendar, files and accounts, gets to know you, and then looks for things it can take off your plate — booking cars, paying bills, buying groceries, or spotting that you’ve booked a flight but no hotel.

It runs on a model trained specifically for computer use, so it navigates websites itself, and you can watch what it’s doing in a small window. Hark is positioning it as a privacy-focused alternative to the big AI companies, and says AI-native hardware is coming in 2027.

Onboarding was easier than almost any agent I’ve tried — easier than Grok, honestly:

- Sign up for free on the web, or download the iOS or Android app.

- Connect your email — Hark recommends this first, and it’s what makes the proactive features work.

- Add your basic details, like where you are.

- Answer its first question: “What’s one thing on your plate this week I could take off?”

I asked it to book an Italian restaurant for Wednesday next week. It asked how many people and what time — I typed “6pm, two people” with a typo, and it didn’t care — then it started booking one of my actual favourite restaurants. I stopped it before it finished, but it clearly knew what it was doing.

- Integrations — Gmail plus Slack, GitHub, LinkedIn, Notion, Amazon, PayPal and more, and you can add a wallet.

- Proactive inbox — it reads your emails and suggests action items you approve or dismiss.

- Panels — custom mini-apps for anything: workouts, calories, productivity, calendar events, Shopify packages, new podcast episodes.

- Home — your spaces, panels and action buttons in one place, including paying bills.

- Projects — dedicated threads with their own files for long-horizon work, like planning an event or tracking a topic.

- Scheduled tasks — manage recurring jobs you set up in chat.

- Voice input and attachments — voice is input only; it doesn’t talk back yet.

- Prep my day — checks your calendar and inbox and builds the day’s itinerary.

To create a panel, you just describe it. I typed “track my productivity” and it asked whether I meant meeting hours versus focus time, or tasks from my to-do list — and offered to connect apps like ClickUp or Asana to feed it.

## The Hark AI agent in daily use

The feature I like most is how it uses your connected apps. With some agents, like Grok Bot, you connect an app and then still have to log in again inside the agent’s computer before it can click around. Hark seems to use the apps you’ve integrated directly, which saves time.

“Prep my day” is a great example. It checked my calendar and inbox, told me what was working, that my inbox was clean, and asked whether I wanted it to pull in the sales numbers before my team sales meeting at 4pm. That’s what a good assistant does — it comes to you.

You can also ask it to plan a trip — where’s good for camping, a packing list, when to leave — and it will start booking flights. The interface is super clean throughout. It honestly feels like the Apple of AI agents — what Apple should have released.

Hark works by getting deep access to your email, calendar, files and even financial accounts. Read its privacy policy, start with your email only, use “stop” when it starts something you didn’t want, and approve purchases and payments yourself.
